<p id="mwQQ">This effect introduces a difference in color <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_(vision)" title="Contrast (vision)" id="mwQg">contrast</a> under different levels of illumination. For instance, in bright <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwQw">sunlight</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelargonium" title="Pelargonium" id="mwRA">geranium</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower" title="Flower" id="mwRQ">flowers</a> appear bright red against the dull <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green" title="Green" id="mwRg">green</a> of their <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf" title="Leaf" id="mwRw">leaves</a>, or adjacent blue flowers, but in the same scene viewed at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dusk" title="Dusk" id="mwSA">dusk</a>, the contrast is reversed, with the red <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petal" title="Petal" id="mwSQ">petals</a> appearing a dark red or black, and the leaves and blue petals appearing relatively bright.</p>

<p id="mwSg">The sensitivity to light in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotopic_vision" title="Scotopic vision" id="mwSw">scotopic vision</a><sup about="#mwt31" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-9" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"lower-alpha"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-9"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"efn","href":"./Template:Efn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"low light conditions"}},"i":0}}]}"><a href="#cite_note-9" data-mw-group="lower-alpha" id="mwTA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwTQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwTg">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwTw">]</span></span></a></sup> varies with wavelength, though the perception is essentially <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white" title="Black-and-white" class="mw-redirect" id="mwUA">black-and-white</a>. The Purkinje shift is the relation between the absorption maximum of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodopsin" title="Rhodopsin" id="mwUQ">rhodopsin</a>, reaching a maximum at about <span about="#mwt34" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwUg" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"500"},"2":{"wt":"nm"}},"i":0}}]}">500 nanometres (2.0</span><span style="margin:0 .15em 0 .25em" about="#mwt34">×</span><span about="#mwt34">10</span><sup about="#mwt34">−5</sup><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt34"> </span><span about="#mwt34">in)</span>, and that of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opsin" title="Opsin" id="mwUw">opsins</a> in the longer-wavelength cones that dominate in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photopic_vision" title="Photopic vision" id="mwVA">photopic vision</a><sup about="#mwt35" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-10" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"lower-alpha"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-10"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"efn","href":"./Template:Efn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"well-lit conditions"}},"i":0}}]}"><a href="#cite_note-10" data-mw-group="lower-alpha" id="mwVQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwVg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwVw">[</span>b<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWA">]</span></span></a></sup>, about <span about="#mwt38" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwWQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"555"},"2":{"wt":"nm"}},"i":0}}]}">555 nanometres (2.19</span><span style="margin:0 .15em 0 .25em" about="#mwt38">×</span><span about="#mwt38">10</span><sup about="#mwt38">−5</sup><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt38"> </span><span about="#mwt38">in)</span> (green).<sup about="#mwt39" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-11" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-11"}}"><a href="#cite_note-11" id="mwWg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwWw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwXA">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwXQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwXg">In visual <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy" title="Astronomy" id="mwXw">astronomy</a>, the Purkinje shift can affect visual estimates of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_star" title="Variable star" id="mwYA">variable stars</a> when viewers use comparison stars of different colors, especially if one of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star" title="Star" id="mwYQ">stars</a> is red.<sup about="#mwt42" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-12" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-12"}}"><a href="#cite_note-12" id="mwYg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwYw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZA">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwZQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" id="mwZg" data-mw="{"autoGenerated":true}"></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwZw" aria-labelledby="Physiology"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Physiology">Physiology</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Purkinje_effect&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Physiology"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwaA">The Purkinje effect occurs at the transition between primary use of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photopic_vision" title="Photopic vision" id="mwaQ">photopic</a> (cone-based) and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotopic_vision" title="Scotopic vision" id="mwag">scotopic</a> (rod-based) systems, that is, in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopic" title="Mesopic" class="mw-redirect" id="mwaw">mesopic</a> state: as intensity dims, the rods take over, and before color disappears completely, it shifts towards the rods' top sensitivity.<sup about="#mwt45" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-13" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-13"}}"><a href="#cite_note-13" id="mwbA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwbQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwbg">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwbw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwcA">The effect occurs because in mesopic conditions the outputs of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_cell" title="Cone cell" id="mwcQ">cones</a> in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina" title="Retina" id="mwcg">retina</a>, which are generally responsible for the perception of color in daylight, are pooled with outputs of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cell" title="Rod cell" id="mwcw">rods</a> which are more sensitive under those conditions and have <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_function" title="Luminosity function" class="mw-redirect" id="mwdA">peak sensitivity</a> in the greenish blue wavelength of 507<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwdQ"> </span>nm.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="2" id="mwdg" aria-labelledby="Use_of_red_lights"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Use_of_red_lights">Use of red lights</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Purkinje_effect&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Use of red lights"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwdw">The insensitivity of rods to long-wavelength (i.e. red) light has led to the use of red lights under certain special circumstances—for example, in the control rooms of submarines, research laboratories, aircraft, and naked-eye astronomy.<sup about="#mwt48" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-14" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-14"}}"><a href="#cite_note-14" id="mweA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mweQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mweg">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwew">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwfA"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwfQ"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg/250px-Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg/500px-Dark_adaptor_goggles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="1632" data-file-height="1232" data-file-type="bitmap" height="189" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwfg"></a><figcaption id="mwfw">Dark adaptor goggles</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwgA">Red lights are used in conditions where it is desirable to activate both the photopic and scotopic systems. Submarines are well lit to facilitate the vision of the crew members working there, but the control room must be lit differently to allow crew members to read instrument panels yet remain dark adjusted to operate the periscope at night. By using red lights or wearing <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_adaptor_goggles" title="Dark adaptor goggles" id="mwgQ">red goggles</a> (called "dark adaptor goggles"), the cones can receive enough light to provide photopic vision (namely the high-acuity vision required for reading). The rods are not saturated by the bright red light because they are not sensitive to long-wavelength light, so the crew members remain dark adapted.<sup about="#mwt51" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-15" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-15"}}"><a href="#cite_note-15" id="mwgg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwgw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwhA">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwhQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Similarly, airplane cockpits use red lights so pilots can read their instruments and maps while maintaining night vision to see outside the aircraft.</p>

<p id="mwhg">Red lights are also often used in research settings. Many research animals (such as rats and mice) have limited photopic vision, as they have far fewer cone photoreceptors.<sup about="#mwt52" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-16" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-16"}}"><a href="#cite_note-16" id="mwhw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwiA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwiQ">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwig">]</span></span></a></sup>
The animal subjects do not perceive red lights and thus experience darkness (the active period for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal" title="Nocturnal" class="mw-redirect" id="mwiw">nocturnal</a> animals), but the human researchers, who have one kind of cone (the "L cone") that is sensitive to long wavelengths, are able to read instruments or perform procedures that would be impractical even with fully dark adapted (but low acuity) scotopic vision.<sup about="#mwt55" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-17" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-17"}}"><a href="#cite_note-17" id="mwjA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwjQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwjg">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwjw">]</span></span></a></sup>
For the same reason, zoo displays of nocturnal animals often are illuminated with red light.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="3" id="mwkA" aria-labelledby="History"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History">History</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Purkinje_effect&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: History"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p id="mwkQ">The effect was discovered in 1819 by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Evangelista_Purkyně" title="Jan Evangelista Purkyně" id="mwkg">Jan Evangelista Purkyně</a>. Purkyně was a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymath" title="Polymath" id="mwkw">polymath</a><sup about="#mwt56" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-wade_18-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"wade"}}"><a href="#cite_note-wade-18" id="mwlA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwlQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwlg">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwlw">]</span></span></a></sup> who would often meditate at dawn during long walks in the blossomed <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia" title="Bohemia" id="mwmA">Bohemian</a> fields. Purkyně noticed that his favorite flowers appeared bright red on a sunny afternoon, while at dawn they looked very dark. He reasoned that the eye has not one but two systems adapted to see colors, one for bright overall light intensity, and the other for dusk and dawn.</p>

<p id="mwmQ">Purkyně wrote in his <i id="mwmg">Neue Beiträge:</i><sup about="#mwt59" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-wade_18-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"wade"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-wade-18"}}"><a href="#cite_note-wade-18" id="mwmw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwnA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwnQ">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwng">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt62" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-19" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-19"}}"><a href="#cite_note-19" id="mwnw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwoA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwoQ">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwog">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<blockquote id="mwow"><p id="mwpA">Objectively, the degree of illumination has a great influence on the intensity of color quality. In order to prove this most vividly, take some colors before daybreak, when it begins slowly to get lighter. Initially one sees only black and grey. Particularly the brightest colors, red and green, appear darkest. Yellow cannot be distinguished from a rosy red. Blue became noticeable to me first. Nuances of red, which otherwise burn brightest in daylight, namely carmine, cinnabar and orange, show themselves as darkest for quite a while, in contrast to their average brightness. Green appears more bluish to me, and its yellow tint develops with increasing daylight only.</p></blockquote>
